newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal central bank probes Nazi gold deposits.
newsitem.headline: Portugal central bank probes Nazi gold deposits.

text.p: Portugal's central bank, under fire for accumulating Nazi gold during World War Two, said on Thursday it had appointed an independent investigator into its past activities.
Economic historian Joaquim da Costa Leite from Lisbon's Universidade Nova will go through the bank's records between 1939 and 1945, a bank spokesman told Reuters.
He will have to work within the limits of a law preventing the publication of sensitive documents until 50 years after the death of those involved.
"The historian will research documents from the period and bring to light what happened, within the limits of the law," the spokesman said.
Local historians and Jewish groups have long urged the government to end the restriction and lift the veil on the period when Portugal was ruled by right-wing dictator Antonio Salazar.

The Bank of Portugal has admitted that the country took delivery of gold from Nazi Germany during World War Two, but it has denied that it was used to launder or hide gold stolen from Jewish victims of Nazi Germany.
It says the gold was payment for Portuguese exports, particularly of wolfram which is used in explosives.
But recently-released U.S. government documents suggest that Portugal acquired looted gold worth about $1 billion at today's prices and tried to used it to buy Polish coal in the winter of 1946.
The attempt spurred fierce protests from the United States, Britain and France which wanted the gold returned to its rightful owners.

Switzerland, also neutral during the war, has seen the reputation of its financial centre tarnished by accusations its banks robbed Holocaust victims. It has set up a commission to look into its financial dealings with Nazi Germany.

Although Portugal was officially neutral, Salazar was often accused of being a Nazi sympathiser. He provoked international outrage when he ordered flags to be flown at half mast on Adolf Hitler's death.
The central bank sold hundreds of tonnes of gold after Portugal's 1974 revolution, which overthrew the Salazar regime, in order to meet foreign debt payments.
